messages.author: 39928757d2a23fb4
messages.subject: Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have a question that is primarily conceptual, and which has implications at the empirical level as well. Since I am getting familiar with QCA, I welcome any questions/clarifications, and apologize if I don't always use the appropriate terminology.

I have a dataset containing 16 variables that relate to a binary outcome, ADOPT to indicate if users adopt a technology of not. I have 95 observations in total.

Each of the 16 conditions, as well as ADOPT, are categorical rather than continuous (e.g., Yes/No answers). The majority of variables in the dataset is measured as binary directly from the source (i.e., V1 {0,1}, V2 {0,1}, ADOPT {0,1}). Those are easy to calibrate as crisp sets.

There are a few conditions however, that can take on one of 3 values, e.g., {Low, Medium, High}. From what I read in the QCA with R book (which is excellent for novices by the way!), I could technically model those as fuzzy sets since I could argue that there is a gradation of full membership from Low to High. For other conditions, it's less clear  and I have resorted to using crisp sets with values {0, 1, 2} to denote the 3 possible values for the condition. 

Here are my questions given this situation:
  1. Would running the analysis with a combination of crisp and fuzzy be ok?
  2. Are there specific things I should watch out for regarding multi-valued sets? I have read a few sources that seem to recommend exercising caution. As I read through them, I did try to implement a solution where the possible values are instead broken down into 3 dummy variables, but the truth table cannot be generated, giving the error "Running a QCA analysis with so many conditions is difficult." in those cases,

Anyway I am just trying to make sure I tackle this right at the conceptual level first before I try to move into operationalization too much.

Thanks in advance! I'll be happy to post files or provide clarifications if needed.

messages.author: 53dbab5845ace6b6
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Hi Greg,

To answer your questions point by point:

1. Yes, the analysis would run on any combination of crisp, fuzzy and multi-value. The R package QCA is happy to accept whatever you have for the explanatory conditions. So not just crisp and fuzzy, you can absolutely use crisp and multi-value. If the condition is multi-value, I would say no, do not convert it to fuzzy sets just because some sources recommend caution (I would be interested to read those sources).

2. Nothing specific to watch out for, the analysis should just run. 16 conditions may seem a lot, but in fact I ran a minimization for 100 conditions and it still works. True though, at that number of conditions it is very likely you will get extreme model ambiguity, that is millions to an infinite number of different possible ways to solve the PI chart. Whether you consider that a successful analysis or not, it's up to you (for me, having millions of possible solutions is effectively saying "any explanation holds").

Truth tables should not be a problem to construct, even for 16 conditions out of which some are multi-value. Please send a reproducible example and I will have a look, if it still doesn't work. There would be more things to say about such an analysis: I normally would not recommend using more than 7-8 conditions, not because of algorithm limitations (it can do a whole lot more), but because of conceptual complexity of the explanatory model. I suspect you're running an exploratory exercise (see which conditions survive, to analyze later) but on extreme model ambiguity you might not get a very definitive answer.

All the best,
Adrian

messages.author: df5468b8c5e117c8
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Hiya Greg,

The more serious concern is that 16 conditions and only 95 observations produce overwhelming limited diversity. That's even worse when some of the conditions are multi-value, which increases even more the number of possible logical configurations. Dummy-coding one condition into three additional conditions further aggravates the problem by creating logically impossible configurations (for example, a configuration combining the presence of two or more of those newly created conditions; think of a traffic light that is both red AND green).

Honestly, if I were you, I would first reduce the number of conditions to something more manageable. I'm even stricter than Professor Dușa, and would not recommend using more than 5, especially if any of them are multi-value.

But keep in mind that I'm biased, because I hate mvQCA and avoid it at all costs! It creates more problems than it solves.

Breno

messages.author: 39928757d2a23fb4
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Hi Adrian,

Thank you for the prompt reply.

To answer your question, this is one source I had been reading is the following: Vink, M. P., & Van Vliet, O. (2009). Not quite crisp, not yet fuzzy? Assessing the potentials and pitfalls of multi-value QCA. Field Methods, 21(3), 265-289.

The article is one in a series of conversations on the topic, and the authors do look at both sides of the argument as well. I was more wondering about the ability to combine different types of sets into the analysis when I first stumbled upon it.

Onto your answer to my second question, this is where I think the conceptual part of really important before assessing the computation itself. Just thinking about the number of conditions and cases to cover all possible combinations really affects the ability to interpret any results. This is something I am going to keep on reading about as I try and explore the data further. One issue I have run into has been to use the superSubset() function while specifying  incl.cut = 0.9. This gives me an error (" INTEGER() can only be applied to a 'integer', not a 'double' ") , but putting a value of 0.8 works. 

After minimization, my solution incorporates quite a few recipes so I know there is definitely more work to do. Most of which I expect to be initially conceptual rather than analytical.

But it's definitely an interesting approach to get into!

parts:
Breno, Greg,

I wouldn't say mvQCA creates more problems than it solves. To me, and this is going to become part of the future theoretical description, QCA explanatory conditions are actually categories.
And it so happens that mv conditions are special types of crisp with more than two categories, and it sometimes makes sense to bring all these (mutually exclusive) categories into one mv condition, rather than creating multiple binary separate conditions. But that is a much longer discussion, and I hope to write a material about this.

With all my best,
Adrian

messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Greg,

Yeah, reducing the number of theoretically relevant conditions when many are present is always tricky. One possibility is to examine whether some are components or alternative manifestations of broader concepts. You could then construct higher-order sets using theoretically justified set operations. For example, if the literature defines membership in a broader concept as requiring all its components, the higher-order set would be their conjunction. Conversely, if any one of several components is sufficient for membership in the broader concept, the higher-order set would be their disjunction.

Here is a small example with mock binary data:

```
set.seed(4)

foo <- as.data.frame(
  matrix(
    sample(0:1, 60, replace = TRUE),
    ncol = 5,
    dimnames = list(
      paste0("Case", seq_len(12)),
      c("V1", "V2", "V3", "V4", "OUT")
    )
  )
)

library(QCA)

# Both V1 and V2 are required for membership in V1andV2
foo$V1andV2 <- fuzzyand(foo$V1, foo$V2)

# Either V3 or V4 is sufficient for membership in V3orV4
foo$V3orV4 <- fuzzyor(foo$V3, foo$V4)

tt <- truthTable(
    foo,
    outcome = "OUT",
    conditions = c("V1andV2", "V3orV4"),
    incl.cut = 0.8,
    n.cut = 1,
    show.cases = TRUE
)

tt

minimize(
    tt,
    include = "?",
    details = TRUE
)
```

It's an idea!

Breno

On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 3:55 PM Adrian Dușa <dusa....@gmail.com> wrote:
Breno, Greg,

I wouldn't say mvQCA creates more problems than it solves. To me, and this is going to become part of the future theoretical description, QCA explanatory conditions are actually categories.
And it so happens that mv conditions are special types of crisp with more than two categories, and it sometimes makes sense to bring all these (mutually exclusive) categories into one mv condition, rather than creating multiple binary separate conditions. But that is a much longer discussion, and I hope to write a material about this.

With all my best,
Adrian

messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Question about multi-value QCA
parts:
Breno, Adrian,

Thank you for the detailed answers and for the insights into the methods and tradeoffs, it really helps to better understand things. Although I have to say again that the book is really well put together.

I also see multi-valued sets as a generic version of binary sets, with the latter offering a lot more ease because the dichotomy solves some of the headaches related to how you operationalize three possible values.

Maybe to explain a bit more how the project works, I can provide some high level overview to illustrate how I get where I am. I have a list of (16) conditions that contribute to explain a binary outcome, which are informed by literature. The conditions are, for some of them, binary, for others, more like categorical or ordinal variables (e.g., Low, Medium, High). So the point is that, theoretically at least, it makes sense to have multi-value sets for those. Already, the categorical vs ordinal aspect can be tricky because with an ordinal variable, you could already think of "medium" as indicating set membership (a bit like the example where an orange light is already considered to be red for many traffic violations in some countries).

The other thing is that series of conditions relate to the same overarching category, a bit like a formative construct's dimensions (I know the comparison is not right, but for lack of better word this is how I am picturing it). Each category is theoretically distinct such that conditions cannot be related to more than one category.

After thinking a bit about your replies, I see some things that I could try, given the fact that with 16 conditions, some of which have 3 possible values, and 95 observations, the solution will just not make much sense (which is where I am pretty much already from early analyses).

The main one at this point would be to try a "per-category" QCA which, for each category, will basically have 3 or 4 conditions. And then, with some theory-informed operationalizations (TBD), do a general QCA with each category that will be built on its conditions. But basically, it's a 2 step QCA that abstracts away from the details. This may make absolutely no sense, I am just thinking out loud here :). But I think this is what Breno is suggesting, although I am not sure how that would work with non-binary sets.

Greg
